issues.legal_issue: A Magistrate’s decision to initiate possession proceedings rests on the Magistrate’s satisfaction from the available information, and a revisional court does not reassess the sufficiency of the material where the Magistrate records the facts supporting that satisfaction.
material_facts: The applicant alleged forcible and wrongful dispossession and a likelihood of breach of the peace.
The Magistrate examined the applicant on oath, considered the facts in the application and recorded satisfaction that a dispute existed.
issues.conclusion: The Magistrate’s satisfaction was based on prima facie material, and the revisional court was not entitled to set aside the order by reassessing whether that material was sufficient. The facts stated in the application and the examination on oath supplied the reasons for the Magistrate’s satisfaction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 145(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 requires the Magistrate to be satisfied that a dispute concerning immovable property exists and is likely to cause a breach of the peace, and requires reasons to be recorded. The satisfaction is the Magistrate’s, exercised according to law; no fixed rule governs the sufficiency of the material, and revisional jurisdiction does not extend to reassessing its sufficiency. The facts recorded as the basis for satisfaction may themselves constitute the reasons.

rule.if: possession_dispute_proceeding and magistrate_recorded_satisfaction and magistrate_examined_applicant_on_oath and application_facts_supported_satisfaction

predicates.possession_dispute_proceeding: The proceeding concerned a dispute over possession of immovable property that was said to risk a breach of the peace.
predicates.magistrate_recorded_satisfaction: The Magistrate stated that the required conditions for initiating the proceeding were present.
predicates.magistrate_examined_applicant_on_oath: The Magistrate examined the applicant on oath before initiating the proceeding.
predicates.application_facts_supported_satisfaction: The facts stated in the applicant’s application supplied prima facie support for the Magistrate’s satisfaction.

issues.definition: When a possession-dispute proceeding is initiated on a recorded satisfaction supported by application facts after the applicant is examined on oath, the preliminary order is not set aside merely because a revisional court considers the material insufficient.

issues.legal_issue: A Magistrate may initiate possession proceedings on an application or other information without first obtaining a police report.
material_facts: The applicant applied for proceedings after alleging forcible dispossession, threats and an assault.
Before making the preliminary order, the Magistrate examined the applicant on oath and had the application’s allegations and information about the applicant’s police complaints before him.
issues.conclusion: The Magistrate was not required to obtain a police report before acting on the application and other information.
issues.legal_principle: Section 145(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 permits the Magistrate to act on a police report or on other information, which includes an application by a private party. The Magistrate must act cautiously because the jurisdiction is of an emergency nature, but a police report is not a prerequisite once the Magistrate is satisfied that the statutory conditions exist. The Court disapproved the contrary views in Phutania v. Emperor and Ganesh v. Venkataswara; it explained that Raja of Karvetnagar v. Sowcar Lodd Govind Doss called for caution about relying on an interested party’s statements, not a mandatory police report.

rule.if: possession_dispute_proceeding and private_application_received and magistrate_examined_applicant_on_oath and magistrate_satisfied_requirements_exist

predicates.possession_dispute_proceeding: The proceeding concerned a dispute over possession of immovable property that was said to risk a breach of the peace.
predicates.private_application_received: A party to the possession dispute applied to the Magistrate for proceedings.
predicates.magistrate_examined_applicant_on_oath: The Magistrate examined the applicant on oath before initiating the proceeding.
predicates.magistrate_satisfied_requirements_exist: The Magistrate was satisfied that a possession dispute existed and was likely to cause a breach of the peace.

issues.definition: When a party applies in a possession-dispute proceeding and the Magistrate is satisfied after examining the applicant on oath that the required conditions exist, proceedings may begin without a police report.

issues.legal_issue: A completed forcible and wrongful dispossession shortly before a preliminary order does not eliminate the dispute or prevent the Magistrate from treating the dispossessed party as in possession and restoring possession.
material_facts: The Magistrate found that the applicant had been in actual possession and had been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed.
The dispossession occurred within two months before the preliminary order.
The Magistrate directed restoration of possession to the applicant until eviction in due course of law.
issues.conclusion: The dispossession’s completion before the preliminary order did not prevent the Magistrate from proceeding or ordering restoration. Because the dispossession occurred within the relevant two-month period, the applicant was deemed to have been in possession on the date of the preliminary order.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to section 145(4) and section 145(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 allow a party forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed within two months before the preliminary order to be treated as in possession on that order’s date and permit restoration until eviction in due course of law. The proviso prevents the law from recognising the advantage of a completed forcible dispossession. The Court applied Edwick v. Hawkes, Jiba v. Chandulal, A. N. Shah v. Nageswara Rao and Subarna Sunami v. Kartika Kudal.

rule.if: possession_dispute_proceeding and initial_breach_risk_found and forcible_wrongful_dispossession_found and dispossession_within_recent_period

predicates.possession_dispute_proceeding: The proceeding concerned a dispute over possession of immovable property that was said to risk a breach of the peace.
predicates.initial_breach_risk_found: The Magistrate was satisfied when initiating the proceeding that the dispute was likely to cause a breach of the peace.
predicates.forcible_wrongful_dispossession_found: The Magistrate found that one party had forcibly and wrongfully removed another from possession.
predicates.dispossession_within_recent_period: The forcible and wrongful dispossession occurred within the two months preceding the preliminary order.

issues.definition: When a recent forcible and wrongful dispossession is found in a possession-dispute proceeding initiated on an apprehended breach of the peace, the dispossessed party is treated as in possession and restoration may be ordered.

issues.legal_issue: The apprehension of a breach of the peace need not continue when the Magistrate makes the final possession order if the required conditions existed when proceedings were initiated.
material_facts: The Magistrate was satisfied before initiating the proceeding that a dispute existed and was likely to cause a breach of the peace.
The alleged dispossession was complete and a police complaint had been made before the preliminary order.
After the inquiry, the Magistrate made a final order on possession.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a continuing apprehension of a breach of the peace at the final-order stage did not prevent the Magistrate from completing the inquiry and making the final order.
issues.legal_principle: Under the scheme of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the conditions of an existing dispute and likelihood of a breach of the peace must be satisfied before proceedings are initiated. Once they are satisfied and the preliminary order is made, the Magistrate must conduct the inquiry under section 145(4) and make the final order under section 145(6); a continuing apprehension at the final-order stage is unnecessary.

rule.if: possession_dispute_proceeding and initial_breach_risk_found and preliminary_order_made and final_inquiry_completed

predicates.possession_dispute_proceeding: The proceeding concerned a dispute over possession of immovable property that was said to risk a breach of the peace.
predicates.initial_breach_risk_found: The Magistrate was satisfied when initiating the proceeding that the dispute was likely to cause a breach of the peace.
predicates.preliminary_order_made: The Magistrate made a preliminary order after finding the conditions for initiating the proceeding satisfied.
predicates.final_inquiry_completed: The Magistrate completed the inquiry into possession before making the final order.

issues.definition: When a possession-dispute proceeding was initiated on a finding of an apprehended breach of the peace and the inquiry is completed, a final order is permitted even if that apprehension no longer continues.
